National Observatory of Athens / METEO unit Seasonal climate outlook for Europe November 2025 Contents 1 Introduction 2 2 State of the climate 3 3 Seasonal outlook 5 4 Monthly-mean 2m-temperature anomaly 6 5 Cold month probability 7 6 Warm month probability 8 7 Monthly Frost Days count 9 8 Monthly Frost Days count anomaly 10 9 Monthly Warm Days count 11 10 Monthly Warm Days count anomaly 12 11 Monthly precipitation accumulation anomaly 13 12 Dry month probability 14 13 Wet month probability 15 14 Soil moisture anomaly 16 Acknowledgements 17 References 17 1 1 Introduction Seasonal climate forecasting aims to estimate how likely it is for a particular geographical region to experience warmer or colder and wetter or drier than average conditions in the coming months. This is crucial information for weather-sensitive sectors like agriculture. Despite the chaos in the atmosphere, getting such a glimpse into the future is possible due to the presence of slowly-evolving fields (e.g., sea surface temperature, soil moisture, snow cover) and phenomena (e.g., ENSO) in the Earth system.
Given the pronounced and unavoidable uncertainty in predicting the long-term evolution of the Earth system, seasonal forecasts have to be probabilistic. To that end, probabilistic estimates about the average weather conditions in the months ahead are derived by running one or, ideally, several different models multiple times to produce an ensemble of equiprobable outcomes.
Despite the ever-growing availability and accessibility of seasonal forecasts, it has to be emphasized that these long-term forecasts are characterized by significant uncertainty and aim to estimate the tendency in the monthly and seasonal evolution of average weather conditions. Daily and local weather conditions may differ significantly from the monthly average conditions in a broader region. November 2025
   On November 9–10, an early-season lake-effect snow event brought localized accumulations of up to a foot to parts of northeast Illinois and northwest Indiana.
   On November 29–30, a powerful post-Thanksgiving storm dropped heavy snow across the Midwest. Chicago O’Hare Airport in Illinois recorded 8.4 inches on November 29, the highest single-day November snowfall on record.
   An Arctic blast on November 10–11 brought the earliest snow on record to Wilmington and Lumberton, NC.
   An Arctic air mass brought record cold to the Deep South November 11–14, with dozens of stations setting daily minimum records, including a low of 28°F in Jacksonville, FL. For the year, the CONUS average maximum temperature was 66.63°F, which was 2.65°F above average and ranked as the fifth-warmest year for daytime high temperatures in the 131-year record. The average minimum (nighttime) temperature was 42.62°F, 2.59°F above average, ranking eighth-warmest on record.

[...] The Northeast's annual average temperature for 2025 was 48.1°F, 0.3°F warmer than normal. Eleven of the 12 Northeast states experienced a warmer-than-normal year. Average temperatures for all states ranged from 0.3°F below normal in Delaware, the lone cooler-than-normal state, to 0.5°F above normal in Connecticut, Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, and West Virginia. 2025 ranked among the 20 warmest years on record for seven states: Maine, 17th warmest; New Hampshire, 18th warmest; Maryland, Rhode Island, and Vermont, 19th warmest; and Connecticut and Massachusetts, 20th warmest.
